title: Market Outlook:
intro:
Market Outlook:
Wall Street Diverges as Oil Risks, AI Concerns and Inflation Take Centre Stage
US equities ended mixed in thin holiday trading, with energy stocks outperforming as geopolitical tensions supported crude prices, while technology shares came under pressure amid renewed concerns over AI spending and rising financing costs. Investors are now turning their attention to major bank earnings and key US inflation data, which could influence expectations for the Federal Reserve’s next policy moves.

US Equities: Rotation Away from Technology
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.38% to 51,850.55, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.06% to 7,807.24 and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.44% to 27,245.90.
The session highlighted a divergence beneath the surface of the broader market. Eight of the eleven S&P 500 sectors advanced, led by energy, which gained 1.44%. Technology was the weakest sector, falling 1.22% as investors reassessed the sustainability of AI-related spending and the impact of higher borrowing costs.

Competition from China’s CXMT in memory-chip technology added to concerns surrounding the semiconductor industry. Several technology stocks suffered sharp losses, including Lumentum and Ciena, while SanDisk declined despite receiving a credit-rating upgrade.

However, weakness was not uniform across the sector. Meta gained 3.38%, supported by developments in its AI models, while Salesforce and Manhattan Associates also advanced. The market is increasingly distinguishing between companies able to demonstrate tangible growth from AI investments and those more exposed to elevated valuations and uncertain returns.

Oil and Energy: Geopolitical Risk Remains Elevated
Energy stocks outperformed as Brent crude gained 1.8% to $106.65 per barrel, supported by escalating tensions in the Middle East and renewed Russian strikes against Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The situation remains complex. The announcement of a Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire and an agreement involving Russian diesel exports had the potential to ease supply concerns. However, continued attacks on energy infrastructure and uncertainty surrounding the implementation of these arrangements have limited the market’s confidence in a lasting improvement.
Russia’s partial relaxation of diesel export restrictions could provide some relief to refined-product markets, but the effect on overall energy prices will depend on actual export volumes, logistics and the persistence of disruptions elsewhere.
Meanwhile, tensions involving Saudi Arabia, Iran-backed Houthi militants and the wider Middle East continue to represent an additional source of supply risk.
For traders, the key distinction remains between a geopolitical risk premium and a sustained deterioration in physical supply.
Oil can remain volatile even when diplomatic agreements suggest that conditions should improve.

US Dollar, Gold and Treasury Yields: Inflation Takes Priority
The US dollar index hovered around 102.5, near its strongest level since April 2025, supported by safe-haven demand and expectations that the Federal Reserve may need to maintain a restrictive monetary stance.
Gold remained below $4,200 an ounce, facing pressure from the stronger dollar and uncertainty ahead of the latest US inflation figures.
The Consumer Price Index, due Wednesday, and Producer Price Index, scheduled for Thursday, are the main macroeconomic events to watch. Stronger-than-expected inflation could reinforce expectations of higher interest rates, supporting the dollar and weighing on gold and other rate-sensitive assets. Softer readings could ease pressure on precious metals and risk assets.

The US 10-year Treasury yield fell below 5.2%, retreating from recent multi-year highs as the bond-market selloff lost momentum. Nevertheless, yields remain a critical variable for equities: persistently elevated borrowing costs could put further pressure on technology valuations and companies dependent on future earnings growth.
Markets are also focused on the Federal Reserve’s next decisions. Expectations of a prolonged restrictive policy stance leave little room for complacency if inflation proves more persistent than anticipated.

Bank Earnings: The Next Test for Wall Street
Major US banks, including JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, Wells Fargo and Goldman Sachs, are scheduled to report earnings
Tuesday, followed by additional financial-sector results later in the week.
Investors will focus on trading revenues, net interest income, loan demand, credit quality and management guidance.
The results should offer a useful assessment of how higher interest rates and tighter financial conditions are affecting both banks and their customers.
Strong results could support financial stocks and help stabilise broader market sentiment.
Conversely, weaker guidance or signs of deteriorating credit quality could add to concerns about the economic outlook.

Intermarket Outlook and Trading Bias
The current market environment is characterised by conflicting forces: geopolitical tensions are supporting energy prices, higher yields and a stronger dollar are challenging growth-sensitive assets, and uncertainty surrounding AI valuations is creating selective pressure within technology.

The main transmission mechanism to monitor is:
Oil prices higher → inflation risks increase → Treasury yields remain elevated → dollar supported → pressure on gold and high-valuation equities.
This relationship is not automatic, but it provides a useful framework for interpreting the next market moves.
Overall Bias: Equities remain vulnerable to further technology-sector weakness, although sector rotation is helping prevent a broader sell-off. The dollar retains a supportive backdrop while inflation and interest-rate expectations remain firm. Oil faces continued upside risks from geopolitical developments, while gold needs relief from dollar strength and yields to regain momentum.

The immediate focus is on US CPI, followed by PPI and bank earnings. These catalysts should help determine whether the recent divergence across asset classes develops into a broader market correction or remains a selective rotation between sectors.
